title: The History of Anti-Communism
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Anti-communism is the opposition to communist ideas and groups. It started after the Russian Revolution in 1917. Many different people and groups have been anti-communist. This includes people with many different political views. It also includes some religious groups and people who make art or write books.
pages.caption: A widely publicized election poster of the Social Democratic Party of Germany from 1932, with the Three Arrows symbol representing resistance against reactionary conservatism, Nazism and Communism, alongside the slogan "Against Papen, Hitler, Thälmann"

evidence.fileTitle: File:Three Arrows election poster of the Social Democratic Party of Germany, 1932 - Gegen Papen, Hitler, Thälmann.png
evidence.articleCaption: A widely publicized election poster of the Social Democratic Party of Germany from 1932, with the Three Arrows symbol representing resistance against reactionary conservatism, Nazism and Communism, alongside the slogan "Against Papen, Hitler, Thälmann"

pages.text: The first group against communism was the White movement in Russia. They fought in a civil war starting in 1918. Other countries helped them. But the Red Army won the war. The Soviet Union was then created in 1922. Anti-communism became a big part of world politics after that.
pages.caption: White propaganda poster "For united Russia" representing the Bolsheviks as a fallen communist dragon and the White cause as a crusading knight (1919)

imageProvenance.credit: ОСВАГ Вооружённых Сил Юга России; Anonymous; Own scan by Vizu.

evidence.fileTitle: File:За единую Россію.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: White propaganda poster "For united Russia" representing the Bolsheviks as a fallen communist dragon and the White cause as a crusading knight (1919)

pages.text: In the United States, anti-communism became strong in 1919. During the 1930s, many groups in America and Europe opposed communism. Some fascist governments also fought against it. Countries like Japan and China had strong anti-communist forces too. They formed alliances to stop the spread of communist ideas.
pages.caption: The Freikorps were anti-communist right-wing paramilitaries (which were essential in fighting against and dismantling the communist revolution in Germany between 1918 and 1919) who are widely seen as a precursor to Nazism and responsible for the assassination of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.

imageProvenance.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Unknown authorUnknown author

evidence.articleCaption: The Freikorps were anti-communist right-wing paramilitaries (which were essential in fighting against and dismantling the communist revolution in Germany between 1918 and 1919) who are widely seen as a precursor to Nazism and responsible for the assassination of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.

pages.text: After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals. This was the Cold War. The United States helped many countries fight communism. There were wars in places like Korea and Vietnam. A group called NATO was created to be an anti-communist military alliance in 1949.
pages.caption: Propaganda poster of the Russian Whites, contrasting its positive ideal of a "Holy" Christian Russia to Soviet Russia of the Bolsheviks; the Bolsheviks are marked with Jewish facial traits

evidence.fileTitle: File:Volunteer Army poster.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Propaganda poster of the Russian Whites, contrasting its positive ideal of a "Holy" Christian Russia to Soviet Russia of the Bolsheviks; the Bolsheviks are marked with Jewish facial traits

pages.text: The Cold War ended when the Soviet Union stopped existing in 1991. Most communist governments were replaced. However, anti-communism is still a part of politics today. Some groups still work against the communist government in China and other places. It remains a topic in many countries around the world.

Anti-communism is the political and ideological opposition to communist beliefs and groups. While it gained global attention during the Cold War, it began much earlier. Organized resistance emerged following the 1917 October Revolution in Russia. Since then, it has appeared across the political spectrum, from anarchism to social democracy.
pages.caption: A widely publicized election poster of the Social Democratic Party of Germany from 1932, with the Three Arrows symbol representing resistance against reactionary conservatism, Nazism and Communism, alongside the slogan "Against Papen, Hitler, Thälmann"

pages.text: The Russian White movement was the first organization dedicated to opposing communism. It fought the Bolshevik government during the Russian Civil War starting in 1918. Although foreign governments provided military support, the White movement was defeated. The Soviet Union was established in 1922, and anti-communism became a major global movement.
pages.caption: White propaganda poster "For united Russia" representing the Bolsheviks as a fallen communist dragon and the White cause as a crusading knight (1919)

pages.text: During the 1920s and 1930s, opposition to communism grew in the United States and Europe. Conservatives, liberals, and fascists all opposed communist growth. In 1936, Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan formed the Anti-Comintern Pact. This alliance was specifically designed to counter the influence of international communist organizations during that period.
pages.caption: The Freikorps were anti-communist right-wing paramilitaries (which were essential in fighting against and dismantling the communist revolution in Germany between 1918 and 1919) who are widely seen as a precursor to Nazism and responsible for the assassination of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.

pages.text: After 1945, the Cold War began between the United States and the Soviet Union. The U.S. government supported global anti-communism as part of its containment policy. This led to military conflicts in Korea, Vietnam, and Afghanistan. In 1949, Western nations founded NATO to serve as an anti-communist military alliance.

pages.text: The Cold War ended with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. Most communist governments were overthrown during this time. However, anti-communism remains a feature of contemporary politics. Organized movements continue to oppose the government of the People's Republic of China and other remaining communist states today.

Anti-communism encompasses diverse political and ideological opposition to communist governance and theory. Emerging as an organized force following the 1917 Russian Revolution, it transcended specific political labels. It has been adopted by movements ranging from liberalism and social democracy to nationalism and religious groups, reflecting broad resistance to communist influence.

pages.text: The Russian White movement represented the first instance of anti-communism as a formal government policy. Supported by international allies during the Russian Civil War, the movement sought to topple the Bolsheviks. Following the Red Army's victory and the 1922 creation of the Soviet Union, anti-communism evolved into a persistent global political feature.

pages.text: In the interwar period, anti-communism became a central pillar for various factions, including European conservatives and liberals. The 1936 Anti-Comintern Pact between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan formalized this opposition. These forces sought to contain communist expansion, while in Asia, the Kuomintang emerged as a primary anti-communist power during the 1930s.

pages.text: The post-1945 era defined the Cold War, characterized by the rivalry between the capitalist United States and the Marxist–Leninist Soviet Union. U.S. containment policy fueled military interventions in Korea, Vietnam, and elsewhere. The 1949 establishment of NATO provided a permanent institutional framework for Western anti-communist military cooperation during this tense period.

Despite these geopolitical shifts, anti-communism persists as a contemporary political element. Modern movements continue to challenge the legitimacy and policies of remaining communist states, such as the People's Republic of China.

title: Discovering electricity and magnetism
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

A1-A2.headline: The long history of electricity and magnets

pages.text: Long ago, people did not understand lightning, static, or magnets. Ancient civilizations knew that amber attracts light objects and lodestone attracts iron. They also felt shocks from electric fish in rivers, but they did not know these things were connected.
pages.caption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Malapterurus electricus 1.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

pages.text: In later times, people built early machines to create electric sparks. Stephen Gray showed that some materials conduct electricity while others stop it. Researchers also invented the Leyden jar to store large amounts of electrical energy safely inside glass bottles.
pages.caption: Robert Boyle.

evidence.fileTitle: File:The Shannon Portrait of the Hon Robert Boyle.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Robert Boyle.

pages.text: Benjamin Franklin used a kite in a storm to show that lightning is electricity. He then invented the lightning rod to keep buildings safe. Around the same time, people began to understand positive and negative charges clearly.
pages.caption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

evidence.fileTitle: File:P v Musschenbroek t-E.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

pages.text: In 1800, Alessandro Volta built the first device that could make a large electric current, which became known as the battery. This invention gave scientists a new way to study power and test exciting new ideas about energy.
pages.caption: Benjamin Franklin.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Joseph Siffrein Duplessis - Benjamin Franklin - Google Art Project.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Benjamin Franklin.

pages.text: During the nineteenth century, Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry discovered electromagnetic induction. Later, James Clerk Maxwell united electricity and magnetism into a single scientific theory. He wrote equations to explain light, electric fields, and magnetic forces together.

The history of electromagnetic theory began with ancient efforts to explain atmospheric electricity and mysterious natural phenomena. Early civilizations observed that rubbed amber attracts lightweight items and lodestone attracts iron. People also experienced powerful shocks from electric fish, though they could not explain these occurrences.
pages.caption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Malapterurus electricus 1.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

pages.text: During the eighteenth century, researchers improved electric machines using glass balls and plates. Stephen Gray conducted experiments demonstrating the difference between conductors and insulators. Soon afterward, the Leyden jar was invented independently by researchers to store electrical energy in large quantities.
pages.caption: Robert Boyle.

evidence.fileTitle: File:The Shannon Portrait of the Hon Robert Boyle.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Robert Boyle.

pages.text: Benjamin Franklin famously flew a kite through a storm-threatened sky, using a key to charge a Leyden jar and establish the link between lightning and electricity. Following these investigations, he invented the lightning rod, and researchers established the convention of positive and negative electricity.
pages.caption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

evidence.fileTitle: File:P v Musschenbroek t-E.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

pages.text: In 1800, Alessandro Volta constructed the first device capable of producing a large electric current, which later became known as the electric battery. Napoleon later summoned Volta for a command performance of his experiments, awarding him many medals and decorations.
pages.caption: Benjamin Franklin.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Joseph Siffrein Duplessis - Benjamin Franklin - Google Art Project.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Benjamin Franklin.

pages.text: By the nineteenth century, scientists recognized that electricity and magnetism were closely related. Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry independently discovered electromagnetic induction. James Clerk Maxwell subsequently announced his electromagnetic theory, reducing current knowledge into a comprehensive set of differential equations.

Inquiry into electromagnetism originated in antiquity through observations of atmospheric electricity, lodestones, and amber. While ancient civilizations recognized the distinct properties of amber and magnetic iron ore, they lacked a unifying explanatory framework. Similarly, physiological responses to electric fish were widely documented across cultures without any comprehension of a shared electrical origin.
pages.caption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Malapterurus electricus 1.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Electric catfish are found in tropical Africa and the Nile River.

pages.text: Eighteenth-century experimentation advanced significantly through modifications to electric generators and the classification of materials. Stephen Gray empirically distinguished between conductors and non-conductors by testing transmission across long lines. Concurrently, the independent invention of the Leyden jar provided researchers with a reliable capacitor capable of accumulating substantial electrical charges.
pages.caption: Robert Boyle.

evidence.fileTitle: File:The Shannon Portrait of the Hon Robert Boyle.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Robert Boyle.

pages.text: Benjamin Franklin's empirical investigations, most notably his hazardous kite experiment, bridged the conceptual gap between atmospheric lightning and domestic electricity, leading directly to the invention of the lightning rod. This period also saw the establishment of positive and negative electrical nomenclature by figures such as Franklin and Ebenezer Kinnersley.
pages.caption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

evidence.fileTitle: File:P v Musschenbroek t-E.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pieter van Musschenbroek.

pages.text: The transition to sustained current electricity arrived in 1800 when Alessandro Volta constructed the primary apparatus for continuous electrical generation, the battery. Volta's breakthrough drew international acclaim, earning him recognition from Napoleon and numerous prestigious decorations.
pages.caption: Benjamin Franklin.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Joseph Siffrein Duplessis - Benjamin Franklin - Google Art Project.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Benjamin Franklin.

pages.text: Nineteenth-century research culminated in the unification of electrical and magnetic phenomena. Following the independent discoveries of electromagnetic induction by Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry, James Clerk Maxwell formulated his electromagnetic theory of light in 1864. By synthesizing existing knowledge into differential equations, Maxwell successfully integrated magnetic force, electric currents, and electrostatic fields into a comprehensive dynamical framework.

The history of electromagnetic theory began with ancient efforts to explain atmospheric electricity and mysterious natural phenomena. Early civilizations observed that rubbed amber attracts lightweight items and lodestone attracts iron. People also experienced powerful shocks from electric fish, though they could not explain these occurrences.

title: Understanding Climate Change Causes
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The scientific community agrees that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land. The main reason is the greenhouse effect. Gases like carbon dioxide let sunlight in, but they trap heat from the planet.
pages.caption: Brown bars indicate drivers that increase global warming, and blue bars indicate those that decrease global warming. Future global warming potential for long lived drivers like carbon dioxide emissions is not represented.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Physical Drivers of climate change.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Brown bars indicate drivers that increase global warming, and blue bars indicate those that decrease global warming. Future global warming potential for long lived drivers like carbon dioxide emissions is not represented.

pages.text: Carbon dioxide emissions primarily come from burning fossil fuels to provide energy for transport, manufacturing, heating, and electricity. Additional carbon dioxide emissions come from deforestation and industrial processes, which include the greenhouse gases released by the chemical reactions for making cement, steel, aluminum, and fertilizer.
pages.caption: Observed temperature vs the 1850–1900 average used by the IPCC as a pre-industrial baseline. The primary driver for increased global temperatures in the industrial era is human activity, with natural forces adding variability.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Global Temperature And Forces With Fahrenheit.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Observed temperature vs the 1850–1900 average used by the IPCC as a pre-industrial baseline. The primary driver for increased global temperatures in the industrial era is human activity, with natural forces adding variability.

pages.text: Methane comes from livestock, landfills, rice cultivation, and energy extraction. Nitrous oxide comes mostly from fertilizer use. Deforestation also adds carbon dioxide to the air because destroyed trees cannot act as carbon sinks.
pages.caption: A diagram which shows where the extra heat retained on Earth due to the energy imbalance is going.

evidence.articleCaption: A diagram which shows where the extra heat retained on Earth due to the energy imbalance is going.

pages.text: Earth has natural ways to absorb carbon dioxide. Oceans and land plants take in about half of human-caused emissions. However, as warming increases, carbon sinks absorb a smaller fraction of total emissions.
pages.caption: Warming influence of atmospheric greenhouse gases has nearly doubled since 1979, with carbon dioxide and methane being the dominant drivers.

evidence.fileTitle: File:1979- Radiative forcing - climate change - global warming - EPA NOAA.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Warming influence of atmospheric greenhouse gases has nearly doubled since 1979, with carbon dioxide and methane being the dominant drivers.

pages.text: Air pollution creates aerosols that scatter solar radiation. For years, these aerosols caused global dimming and cooled the planet by masking greenhouse warming. Now, pollution controls mean aerosols are declining.

Decades of research have led to a strong scientific consensus: human activity has unequivocally warmed Earth's atmosphere, ocean, and land since pre-industrial times. This warming is primarily driven by the greenhouse effect, where gases trap heat radiating from the planet's surface.
pages.caption: Brown bars indicate drivers that increase global warming, and blue bars indicate those that decrease global warming. Future global warming potential for long lived drivers like carbon dioxide emissions is not represented.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Physical Drivers of climate change.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Brown bars indicate drivers that increase global warming, and blue bars indicate those that decrease global warming. Future global warming potential for long lived drivers like carbon dioxide emissions is not represented.

pages.text: Human-caused emissions come from several major activities. Carbon dioxide emissions primarily result from burning fossil fuels for transport, manufacturing, heating, and electricity. Additional emissions stem from deforestation and industrial processes like producing cement and steel.
pages.caption: Observed temperature vs the 1850–1900 average used by the IPCC as a pre-industrial baseline. The primary driver for increased global temperatures in the industrial era is human activity, with natural forces adding variability.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Global Temperature And Forces With Fahrenheit.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Observed temperature vs the 1850–1900 average used by the IPCC as a pre-industrial baseline. The primary driver for increased global temperatures in the industrial era is human activity, with natural forces adding variability.

pages.text: Other greenhouse gases also play a significant role. Methane emissions are generated by livestock, rice cultivation, landfills, and fossil fuel extraction, while nitrous oxide largely comes from fertilizer decomposition. Meanwhile, changes in land use, especially deforestation, release stored carbon.

title: How Medical Practices Have Evolved
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Medicine is the study of how people stay healthy. It looks at how doctors and treatments have changed over time. Historians study old tools and books to learn how people lived in the past. This helps us understand how we treat sickness and injury today in our world.
pages.caption: A 12th-century manuscript of the Hippocratic Oath in Greek, one of the most famous aspects of classical medicine that carried into later eras

imageProvenance.credit: manuscript:Unknown authorUnknown author scan used in book: Foto de la Biblioteca Vaticana scan from book: User:Rmrfstar

evidence.articleCaption: A 12th-century manuscript of the Hippocratic Oath in Greek, one of the most famous aspects of classical medicine that carried into later eras

pages.text: Long ago, people used plants to heal. In places like Egypt and India, they had their own ways to help the sick. Some early ideas were about magic or religion. People also used special herbs to help with pain. These were the first steps in the history of medicine.
pages.caption: Yarrow, a medicinal plant found in human-occupied caves in the Upper Palaeolithic period

evidence.fileTitle: File:Achillea millefolium 5Dsr 9042.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Yarrow, a medicinal plant found in human-occupied caves in the Upper Palaeolithic period

pages.text: In ancient Greece, doctors thought the body had four fluids. They called these humors. They believed that being sick meant these fluids were not balanced. This idea was used for a very long time. Later, scientists learned that tiny germs are the real cause of many diseases.
pages.caption: A cuneiform terracotta tablet describing a medicinal recipe for poisoning (c. 18th century BCE). Discovered in Nippur, Iraq.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Medical recipe concerning poisoning. Terracotta tablet, from Nippur, Iraq, 18th century BCE. Ancient Orient Museum, Istanbul.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A cuneiform terracotta tablet describing a medicinal recipe for poisoning (c. 18th century BCE). Discovered in Nippur, Iraq.

pages.text: In the Middle Ages, hospitals were often run by nuns. They helped poor people who were sick. Later, the first medical schools opened in Italy. These schools taught students about health. Over time, more people became doctors, and new tools were made to help them perform surgery safely.
pages.caption: Neo-Assyrian cuneiform tablet fragment describing medical text, c. 9th to 7th century BCE

evidence.fileTitle: File:Cuneiform tablet fragment of a medical text c 9 to 7 BCE.png
evidence.articleCaption: Neo-Assyrian cuneiform tablet fragment describing medical text, c. 9th to 7th century BCE

pages.text: Today, medicine is very different. We have new machines and better ways to stop germs. We also have many more women working as nurses and doctors. Medicine continues to change as we learn more. It is a field that keeps growing to help people live better and healthier lives.

The history of medicine explores how human societies have managed health, illness, and injury from prehistory to the present. By studying archaeological evidence and written records, historians track the evolution of medical knowledge. This multidisciplinary field draws on sociology and science to understand how our approach to healing has changed.

pages.text: Early medical traditions emerged in regions like Mesopotamia, Egypt, and India. In ancient India, the Atharvaveda provided early medical knowledge, combining magical charms with herbal remedies. Meanwhile, Mesopotamian practices blended naturalistic and supernatural beliefs. These early systems laid the groundwork for how different cultures viewed the human body and disease.
pages.caption: Yarrow, a medicinal plant found in human-occupied caves in the Upper Palaeolithic period

evidence.articleCaption: Yarrow, a medicinal plant found in human-occupied caves in the Upper Palaeolithic period

pages.text: For centuries, Western medicine relied on the theory of humors, which suggested that four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—controlled health. An imbalance in these fluids was thought to cause illness. This belief persisted until the 19th century, when the germ theory of disease finally replaced it.
pages.caption: A cuneiform terracotta tablet describing a medicinal recipe for poisoning (c. 18th century BCE). Discovered in Nippur, Iraq.

pages.text: During the Middle Ages, monastic hospitals provided basic care for the poor. As knowledge spread, the first medical schools, such as the Schola Medica Salernitana in Italy, began to formalize training. These institutions combined diverse influences from Greek, Latin, and Arabic sources, helping to revive medical study across the Western world.

pages.text: The 20th century transformed medicine through professionalization and new technologies. Research centers connected to hospitals led to breakthroughs like antibiotics and advanced surgery. Furthermore, the field became more inclusive, with women entering the medical profession in greater numbers as nurses and physicians, fundamentally changing the landscape of modern healthcare delivery.

The history of medicine is a multidisciplinary field that documents the evolution of treatments and social systems surrounding health. Historians analyze both archaeological findings and written records to understand how societies have addressed illness. By integrating insights from health sciences and sociology, they map the progression of medical knowledge over time.

pages.text: Ancient civilizations developed distinct healing traditions. In Mesopotamia, medicine was a hybrid of naturalistic and supernatural beliefs. Similarly, early Indian medicine, as recorded in the Atharvaveda, utilized both magical incantations and medicinal herbs. These practices demonstrate the diverse ways early societies attempted to manage health before the advent of modern scientific methods.

pages.text: Western medical thought was long dominated by humoralism, a theory attributed to Galen of Pergamon. This framework posited that health depended on the balance of four bodily fluids. While this theory influenced medicine for centuries, it was eventually superseded in the 19th century by the germ theory, which provided a more accurate understanding of infectious diseases.
pages.caption: A cuneiform terracotta tablet describing a medicinal recipe for poisoning (c. 18th century BCE). Discovered in Nippur, Iraq.

pages.text: Institutional medical education emerged in the 9th century, with the Schola Medica Salernitana serving as a prominent example of international knowledge exchange. These schools synthesized Greek, Arabic, and Hebrew medical traditions. Simultaneously, religious institutions played a critical role in public health, as convents provided essential nursing care to the poor throughout medieval Europe.

pages.text: The 20th century marked a period of rapid professionalization and technological advancement. Innovations in chemistry, genetics, and radiography, alongside the development of antibiotics, redefined medical capabilities. The inclusion of women as nurses and physicians further expanded the profession, establishing the diverse and highly specialized medical systems that characterize modern global healthcare today.

By studying archaeological evidence and written records, historians track the evolution of medical knowledge. This multidisciplinary field draws on sociology and science to understand how our approach to healing has changed.
